Lesson 16 / Part 2 / build-first / ~50 minutes

The Names in a Directory

Three stages. You are given the brief; the code stays folded up until you ask for it.

Reading a directory can fail twice — once when you open it, and again on every entry.
read_dir says so in the types, and ? makes saying so cheap.

Every file this editor has ever opened arrived as a command-line argument, decided before the window existed. Editor::open runs once, from env::args, and after that the list of buffers is fixed — there is no code path anywhere that adds one. This lesson adds the first.

By the end, Ctrl+O lists the directory you started the editor from, and clicking a name opens it in a new tab.

How this variant works

This is lesson 16 turned inside out. The ordinary lesson shows you a change and then explains it. Here every stage gives you the brief first — what to build, where it goes, what it must do, and any idea you could not reasonably invent — and then gets out of the way. You write the code.

Each stage is laid out the same way:

  • The goal — the observable outcome, same as always.
  • What to build — a numbered brief. One item per edit, so you can tally them the way you would tally code blocks.
  • What you'll need — only where the stage turns on something new. Named, not written out.
  • How you'll know — the command to run and what it should say. Get here before you open anything.
  • A hint, folded — the idea you're missing, still no code.
  • The code, folded — what I would have written, and why it is shaped that way. Some of the teaching lives in here, so open it once you're done even if you never got stuck.
The order that makes this worth doing Attempt → compile → hint → attempt again → reveal. Opening the code before you have written something of your own turns this back into the ordinary lesson, minus the explanations. If you are stuck for more than ten minutes, that is what the hint is for — being stuck past that point stops teaching you anything.
Expect compiler errors — two of them are the point Stages 2 and 3 both have a wall in them that this variant deliberately does not warn you about in advance. Hitting error[E0502] yourself and reading what it says is the single most valuable thing on this page. When you get it, read the error before you read the hint.

Before you start

You should be at the end of lesson 15: cargo test reports seventeen passing, and src/main.rs is 620 lines. Two of the three stages below end in a running window; the first ends in a test.

fs and io are already in scope at the top of the file — lessons 2 and 3 put them there. You will not need a new use line anywhere in this lesson.

Type it, don't paste it Doubly so here — there is nothing to paste until you have already written your own. It is about eighty lines this time.

Ask the filesystem what is there

cargo test reports twenty passing.

Before any of this reaches the screen it is a question about data: given a directory, what is in it? That is a function, and a function can be tested — so this stage writes one and proves it, with no UI at all. Two edits.

What to build

  1. A free function list_dir, just above enum Pending. It takes a directory as a &str and hands back the names in it — not the paths, just the names — sorted, as Strings. It can fail, and its type has to say so: io::Result<Vec<String>>. Give it a doc comment.
  2. Three tests at the end of mod tests. One: listing "." finds Cargo.toml. Two: the names come back sorted — check that by cloning the result, sorting the clone, and asserting the two are equal. Three: listing a directory that does not exist is an Err.

cargo test runs with the crate root as the working directory, so "." is the directory holding Cargo.toml. That is what makes the first test stable rather than a guess about your machine.

The third test is the one that would catch a rewrite that swallowed errors. It is easy to write list_dir so that an unreadable directory returns an empty Vec and looks, on screen, exactly like an empty directory. The test says those must stay distinguishable.

What you'll need

std::fs::read_dir is the whole of it. Open that page before you write anything and read the signature — this lesson is partly an exercise in getting the answer from the docs rather than from me.

Count the ways this can fail before you write the body There are two, and they are at different depths. One is the call itself. The other is in the type of what you get back when you iterate it — look at that type carefully, and notice that it is not what a beginner would expect. Neither failure can be ignored, and the compiler will not let you pretend otherwise.

The line you will have to justify

You cannot derive this one, so here it is up front.

A directory entry's file_name() gives an OsString, not a String. A filename on Linux is a bag of bytes that is merely usually UTF-8, and String promises it always is. Those are different claims, so the types are different.

The bridge you want is .to_string_lossy(), which replaces anything that isn't valid UTF-8 with U+FFFD, the replacement character — followed by .into_owned(), because you need a String you can keep rather than a borrow. to_string_lossy cannot fail, which is exactly the problem: a name that has been altered no longer names the file.

Deferred on purpose — lesson 17 breaks this Use it anyway, because String is what the rest of the editor already speaks and changing that is a lesson of its own. Lesson 17 creates a file whose name is not valid UTF-8, watches this picker fail to open it, and replaces String with PathBuf throughout. Write the lossy line knowing it is on borrowed time.

How you'll know

Expect one warning at this stage Nothing calls list_dir from the program yet — only the tests do — so cargo run and cargo clippy will tell you: warning: function `list_dir` is never used. That is correct, and it goes away in stage 2 when the shortcut calls it. It is not something you broke.

cargo test
→ test result: ok. 20 passed; 0 failed

Hint — the shape of the loop, still no code

Build the Vec yourself with a for loop rather than reaching for an iterator chain — the failures are easier to see that way, and you can come back and condense it later.

Iterating what read_dir returns does not give you a directory entry. It gives you a Result containing one, on every iteration. So there is a ? inside the loop as well as one on the call that opened the directory, and the one inside the loop is the surprising one.

Sorting is one line at the end, and Vec already has the method.

The code — open once yours passes, or once you're stuck

adding    existing code, shown only for context

The function, just above enum Pending:

editor/src/main.rsabove the Pending enum

/// The names in a directory, sorted. Not the paths — just the names.
fn list_dir(dir: &str) -> io::Result<Vec<String>> {
    let mut names = Vec::new();
    for entry in fs::read_dir(dir)? {
        names.push(entry?.file_name().to_string_lossy().into_owned());
    }
    names.sort();
    Ok(names)
}
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
enum Pending {

Two failures, two ?s

Look at where the question marks are. There are two, and they are catching different things.

fs::read_dir(dir)? is the first. Opening a directory can fail — it might not exist, or you might not be allowed to look. That returns io::Result<ReadDir>, and ? hands the error back to whoever called us.

entry? is the second, and it is the one worth slowing down for. ReadDir is an iterator, and each item is io::Result<DirEntry> — not DirEntry. Reading a directory is not one operation that succeeds or fails; it is a walk, and the walk can fail partway through, on the fourth entry of nine. The type says so. You cannot write this loop without deciding what happens when it does.

This is the shape you will meet again and again in std: an iterator of Result rather than a Result of an iterator. It exists because the failure is per-item, and flattening it away would be a lie.

Second edit — three tests, at the end of mod tests:

editor/src/main.rsin mod tests, at the end

        assert_eq!(editor.unsaved(), 0);
    }
    #[test]
    fn list_dir_finds_the_crate_manifest() {
        let names = list_dir(".").unwrap();
        assert!(names.contains(&"Cargo.toml".to_owned()));
    }

    #[test]
    fn list_dir_sorts_its_names() {
        let names = list_dir(".").unwrap();
        let mut sorted = names.clone();
        sorted.sort();
        assert_eq!(names, sorted);
    }

    #[test]
    fn list_dir_reports_a_directory_that_is_not_there() {
        assert!(list_dir("no/such/directory").is_err());
    }
}

If yours differs — an iterator chain instead of a loop, a different doc comment, tests named differently — that is fine. What has to match is the signature and the two ?s, because stage 2 calls this and the next lesson rewrites it.

Put the names on screen

Ctrl+O opens a panel listing the directory.

The listing is data the editor holds while a question is on screen — which is exactly the shape of confirm from lesson 15, and it gets the same treatment. Five edits.

What to build

  1. A field on struct Editor holding the listing. Look at how confirm is declared before you write it: something that is only sometimes there, set when the question opens and cleared when it closes. Same wrapper, different payload. Doc-comment it.
  2. Its starting value in Editor::open — nothing is open at start-up.
  3. A Ctrl+O shortcut in fn ui, directly above the Ctrl+W one. Copy the shape of that line. When it fires, call list_dir(".") and match on what comes back: on Ok, store the names; on Err, put cannot read this directory: {error} into the active buffer's status.
  4. A method fn pick(&mut self, ui: &egui::Ui) in impl Editor, just after fn ask. If the field holds a listing, draw an egui::Modal — the same call ask makes, with its own Id — containing the heading Open file, one ui.label per name, and a Cancel button that closes the picker. Nothing is clickable except Cancel yet.
  5. A call to it at the end of fn ui, just after the block that calls ask, and before the frame-time line.

The Err arm in edit 3 is why list_dir returns a Result rather than an empty Vec. A directory you cannot read and a directory with nothing in it are different facts, and only one of them is worth telling the user about. It goes in the status bar, where lesson 3 put the last one.

Unlike ask, pick is worth calling unconditionally and letting it decide for itself whether there is anything to draw. Both are defensible; this one keeps the emptiness check next to the thing that clears it.

What you'll need

Nothing new from egui — Modal, heading, add_space, label and button are all already in fn ask from lesson 15. Read that method first and steal its shape.

Edit 4 is where this stage gets interesting, and I am not going to tell you why in advance. Write the obvious version — the one where Cancel sets the field back to None right there in the closure — and compile it.

How you'll know

cargo run -- a.rs
→ press Ctrl+O
→ a panel titled Open file, listing Cargo.toml, src, target and whatever else is beside them
→ Cancel closes it. The names do nothing yet — they are labels.

Hint — read this after you have hit E0502, not before

The compiler is telling you that you cannot mutate a thing you are in the middle of reading. The closure reads the picker field, so it borrows self for as long as it runs; assigning to that same field inside it is a second, conflicting borrow.

Lesson 15 dodged this by building its question string before the closure started. That dodge does not work here, because the thing you want to change is decided during the closure, by a click.

So use the other one, which you have already written twice: lesson 14's closing variable. Record what happened in a plain local on the stack while the borrow is alive; act on it after the borrow has ended. Decide while you're reading, act once you've stopped.

Fourth — drawing it. This goes in impl Editor, just after fn ask:

editor/src/main.rsin impl Editor, after fn ask

    /// Draw the file picker, and act on what was clicked.
    fn pick(&mut self, ui: &egui::Ui) {
        let mut cancelled = false;

        if let Some(names) = &self.picker {
            egui::Modal::new(egui::Id::new("picker")).show(ui.ctx(), |ui| {
                ui.heading("Open file");
                ui.add_space(8.0);
                for name in names {
                    ui.label(name);
                }
                ui.add_space(8.0);
                if ui.button("Cancel").clicked() {
                    cancelled = true;
                }
            });
        }

        if cancelled {
            self.picker = None;
        }
    }
    /// Write out whatever the pending action is about to throw away.

Why cancelled is a local, not a field

The closure reads self.picker, so it holds a borrow of self for as long as it runs. Setting self.picker = None inside it would be a second, mutable borrow of the same thing — E0502, the error lesson 15 dodged by building its question string before the closure started.

Here the dodge is different and more useful: the closure writes to a plain bool on the stack, and the decision is acted on after the borrow ends. That is lesson 14's closing variable again — decide while you're reading, act once you've stopped — and it is the third time this tutorial has reached for it. It is not a workaround for the borrow checker. It is what the borrow checker was pointing at.

Fifth — call it, at the end of fn ui:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, after the call to ask

        if let Some(pending) = self.confirm {
            self.ask(ui, pending);
        }
        self.pick(ui);
        self.frame_ms = frame_start.elapsed().as_secs_f32() * 1000.0;

Click a name to open it

Clicking a filename opens it in a new tab.

The listing works; the names are inert. Four edits, and three of them are inside fn pick.

What to build

  1. fn open_path(&mut self, path: &str) in impl Editor, above fn close. Two lines: push a Buffer::open(path) onto buffers, and make the new one active. Write it as a method even though it has exactly one caller.
  2. A second local at the top of fn pick, alongside cancelled — this one records which name was clicked, so it is not a bool.
  3. Inside the modal, the names become buttons and record the click.
  4. At the bottom of fn pick, act on it: a clicked name opens and closes the picker; Cancel just closes it. One of the two, not both.

Edit 1 is two lines, and it is the seam the rest of part 2 and the file tree in part 8 are built on. Every way of opening a file ends there, which is why it is a method and not four lines repeated in three places.

Easy to miss — edit 3 changes a line you already have It turns the ui.label(name) line into a button. It is not an added line; it replaces one. Leave the label in place as well and you get every filename twice, once dead and once live.

What you'll need

The same pattern as last stage, carrying a value instead of a flag. And a second wall: the obvious way to hand the clicked name to open_path will not compile, for a reason that is one step on from the last one. Write the obvious version first and read what the compiler says.

How you'll know

cargo clippy --all-targets && cargo test
→ silent, test result: ok. 20 passed; 0 failed

cargo run -- a.rs
→ Ctrl+O, then click Cargo.toml
→ it opens in a new tab, and the tab bar has two entries
→ Ctrl+O again, Cancel: nothing is added

Deferred on purpose — lesson 17 The name is used as a path, which works only because the directory being listed is the one the program is running in. Open the picker, click src, and you get a buffer for a directory — a file that will not read and cannot be saved. Lesson 17 adds the type that knows the difference.
Hint — what the borrow checker is objecting to this time

The local from edit 2 is an Option, and the natural thing to put in it is the name the loop is handing you. But name is a &String borrowed out of the picker field — so keeping it keeps the borrow alive, which is the exact thing the pattern exists to end.

You need a value that outlives the closure, not a reference into what the closure was reading. One method call on name gets you one.

For edit 4: "a name was clicked" and "Cancel was clicked" cannot both be true, and running both arms would push a buffer and then throw the picker away twice. An if let with an else if says that plainly.

The code — four edits, and why one of them clones

First — the method every route into a file will eventually use. In impl Editor, above fn close:

editor/src/main.rsin impl Editor, above fn close

    /// Open a file into a new buffer, and switch to it.
    fn open_path(&mut self, path: &str) {
        self.buffers.push(Buffer::open(path));
        self.active = self.buffers.len() - 1;
    }
    /// Close a buffer, keeping `active` pointing at the file it was on.

Second — somewhere to record the click:

editor/src/main.rsin fn pick, the top

    fn pick(&mut self, ui: &egui::Ui) {
        let mut chosen = None;
        let mut cancelled = false;

Third — the names become buttons, and record what was clicked:

editor/src/main.rsin fn pick, inside the modal

                ui.add_space(8.0);
                for name in names {
                    ui.label(name);
                }
                for name in names {

Fourth — act on it, at the bottom of the same function:

editor/src/main.rsin fn pick, the bottom

        if cancelled {
            self.picker = None;
        }
        if let Some(name) = chosen {
            self.open_path(&name);
            self.picker = None;
        } else if cancelled {
            self.picker = None;

name.clone() is doing real work there. name is a &String borrowed from self.picker, and the whole point of the pattern is that the borrow ends before open_path runs. Keeping the reference would keep the borrow alive and put you straight back into E0502. Cloning one filename is the price of getting out of the closure with the answer.

Where you ended up

700 lines, twenty tests green. One free function, one field, two methods, and a keyboard shortcut.

The finished shape — to diff against, once yours runs

editor/src/main.rsabove the Pending enum

/// The names in a directory, sorted. Not the paths — just the names.
fn list_dir(dir: &str) -> io::Result<Vec<String>> {
    let mut names = Vec::new();
    for entry in fs::read_dir(dir)? {
        names.push(entry?.file_name().to_string_lossy().into_owned());
    }
    names.sort();
    Ok(names)
}

Check yourself

Why does iterating a ReadDir hand you a Result for every entry?

  • Reading a directory can fail partway through it
  • Some entries are directories rather than plain files
  • A filename might not be valid Unicode on this platform
  • The iterator has to report when it reaches the end

Opening the directory is one fallible step and each entry is another — the walk can stop on the fourth of nine. Flattening that into one Result at the front would claim a guarantee the filesystem never made. ↑ Review: two failures, two ?s (stage 1)

Why does the clicked name go into a local variable instead of straight to open_path?

  • The closure is already borrowing what open_path mutates
  • Opening a file inside a closure would block the frame
  • The modal has to be closed before a buffer can be pushed
  • Closures cannot call methods that take &mut self

The closure reads self.picker; open_path needs &mut self. Recording the decision and acting after the borrow ends is the same move as lesson 14's closing — decide while reading, act once you have stopped. ↑ Review: why cancelled is a local (stage 2)

A file in the directory has a name that isn't valid UTF-8. What does this picker do?

  • Shows an altered name that no longer opens the file
  • Skips the entry, so the name never appears
  • Returns an error from list_dir for that entry
  • Opens it correctly — the name is only for display

to_string_lossy substitutes U+FFFD for the invalid bytes and cannot fail. The name you see is not the name on disk, and handing it back as a path finds nothing. Lesson 17 makes the file first and the fix second. ↑ Review: the line you will have to justify (stage 1)

Read this before lesson 17

Primary source: std::fs::read_dir — the function's own documentation, not a tutorial about it. Read the signature, then the "Errors" section, then the example.

This is the habit the mission asks for, practised on something small: the answer to "can this fail, and how" is in the type and the docs, and it took less time to read than to guess. OsString is worth two minutes as well, for why it exists at all.

I'm your teacher here — ask me things. Two in particular. First: tell me how far you got before opening each fold, because that is the only signal I have for whether this format is worth keeping. Second: if your list_dir came out differently from mine and still passes, bring it — a working alternative is worth more discussion than a matching one. The weak point of the lesson itself is the hardcoded ".": you can list one directory and only one. That is deliberate — navigation needs PathBuf, and PathBuf needs the UTF-8 problem explained first — but if it nags at you, try adding a ".." entry before lesson 17 does. You will meet the exact wall the next lesson is about.
